title: Winter energy prices expected to rise to three year high
description: Energy bills for millions of households are expected to rise this winter to the highest level for three years, under a price cap to be announced by th
body: Energy bills for millions of households are expected to rise this winter to the highest level for three years, under a price cap to be announced by the industry regulator on Wednesday.The cap will reflect the rise in the wholesale cost of gas, paid by suppliers and will hit bills just as the colder weather arrives in October until the end of December.Analysts expect Ofgem to say prices will go up by 4% compared with the current cap, affecting those on variable tariffs in England, Scotland and Wales.Firms say energy debt has jumped and, with high bills likely to persist, have called for more support for those struggling to pay. The government says VAT is being cut from electricity bills.The price cap for about 33 million households is expected to rise, driven by volatility in international wholesale gas prices.The average price of gas has been 61% higher over the past three months compared to late 2025, according to suppliers' trade body Energy UK.Millions of people have moved on to fixed energy tariffs, some in response to the uncertainty created by the impact of the US-Israeli war with Iran.Anyone on a fixed deal will not see the price they pay rise, until at least the end of the term of their tariff. About 40% of billpayers have fixed tariffs.Households are paying hundreds of pounds a year more on average than before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 started the energy crisis. Bills have gone up by about 70% compared with the pre-crisis norm, according to industry data.That means unpaid bills and charges have shot up. Energy UK estimates total debt to have collectively risen to £6bn, with an expectation of it to increase to about £7bn by the end of the year.The average billpayer in debt, without a payment plan, owed £3,500, it said.The trade body has called for a flexible discounted tariff for those most in need, funded by taxation. That is supported by many debt charities."Without urgent intervention – namely a national social tariff and implementation of the long-awaited debt write off scheme from Ofgem – we expect this [debt] figure to rise in the coming months, and with that see an increase in the number of people coming to us for help with energy bills," said Emily Whitford, senior public policy advocate at StepChange.The Trades Union Congress has called for a windfall tax on bank profits to be used to reduce energy bills.The government is cutting VAT from electricity bills in October, which should knock about £50 off a typical annual bill, and some policy costs were cancelled or shifted in April, but ministers say there is more to do.Suppliers offer a host of support schemes to anyone struggling to pay, or who is likely to find it difficult.Energy UK has a list of these schemes, external. But it stresses that companies can often only help if you get in touch with your supplier to tell them you are unable to pay.

schema.headline: Winter energy prices expected to rise to three year high

title: Back to school: How to save on uniform costs
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByJemma CrewBusiness reporter Back to school can stir up many emotions for parents, including anxiety about the extra costs
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByJemma CrewBusiness reporter Back to school can stir up many emotions for parents, including anxiety about the extra costs it brings.Almost half of parents said they're worried about the cost of school uniforms, according to research by the charity Save the Children and the Baby Bank Alliance network.And a third of the 2,000 parents polled said they've sacrificed things for themselves to meet back-to-school costs like uniforms, bags or books.New rules limiting the number of items branded with a school logo to three per child come into force in September, aimed at helping ease the financial burden.From baby banks to council grants, here are ways parents can ease the cost of kitting out their kids for school.Your first port of callSave the Children said the new uniform rules are a "good start" but back-to-school costs remain a concern for families across almost all income brackets.The government said schools should make second-hand uniforms accessible to parents."Speak to a teacher you trust, and explain that the costs are difficult," said Megan Meek-O'Connor, head of England and Westminster at Save the Children.Many schools have uniform hubs, swap shops and sales just before term starts, and hardship funds.In London, the School Uniform Reuse Network launched earlier this year, giving schools practical advice to start or improve their own swap shops. During its first term of operation, it saw more than 1,500 items reused across 24 schools.Don't dismiss baby banksParents of older children may not realise a so-called baby bank can help them, but many of the 400 support hubs across the UK provide uniforms for children up to and through secondary school.In its latest survey of members, the Baby Bank Alliance found school uniform was reported as a priority item for the first time.Late summer is one of the busiest times for Little Stars Shrewsbury - just over half the children helped since June have been given uniform support.Image source, Little Stars ShropshireImage caption, Boys' black and grey school trousers sorted into boxes at Little Stars ShropshireHannah Stoddart, operations manager at Little Stars Shrewsbury, said families come to them in varying circumstances. A child starting school might need fully kitting out, while an older pupil may just need to replace one or two items.Stoddart stressed that while the summer holidays "take their toll", the charity provides help all year."So when they've had that growth spurt, when they've scuffed their shoes or they've ripped their trousers or they need a winter coat, that's something they can come back to us for as well," she said.Supermarkets and pre-loved itemsThe relaxed rules on uniform branding mean parents can purchase more items from supermarkets and charity shops, said Save the Children's Meek-O'Connor. Pre-loved items are usually what "kids have grown out of quickly rather than things that are poor quality", she said.Image source, Getty ImagesParents can cheaply stock up on frequent-wear items with supermarket bundle deals, while the charity Family Action suggested they team up to bulk buy items that would otherwise take them over budget.According to research from the bank Nationwide, a third of parents said they buy uniform from supermarkets, a third shop around for the best value and 23% purchase larger sizes so items last longer.Kate Steere, parent and consumer editor at the comparison site Finder, said sports kit costs can be "brutal"."I always encourage parents to tap into their club's community. Families with older kids are usually eager to pass down gear," she said."My boys' football team runs a summer sale for second-hand kit, and apps like Vinted or Facebook Marketplace are goldmines."Check for council grantsYou may be able to get a grant from your local authority if your income is below a certain threshold or you're receiving certain benefits.These can be worth up to £200 per child. Eligibility and how much you can get can vary according to where in the UK you live, so it is best to check with your council directly.Struggling with uniform costs is common and people shouldn't feel ashamed if they need to ask for help, said Meek-O'Connor. "Uniform is supposed to be about making school kind of more accessible, more equal...  it should be something positive," she said.

schema.headline: Back to school: How to save on uniform costs

title: Canada announces 'dollar-for-dollar' retaliatory tariffs on US as high as 50%
description: Canada has announced counter-tariffs as high as 50% on a range of US goods in retaliation to the latest wave of levies on Canadian imports imposed by
body: Canada has announced counter-tariffs as high as 50% on a range of US goods in retaliation to the latest wave of levies on Canadian imports imposed by President Donald Trump last weekend. The Canadian tariffs will apply to nearly C$28bn ($20bn; £15bn) worth of American products, ranging from steel to furniture, fresh tuna and cotton T-shirts, officials announced on Tuesday.The list of targeted products is designed to match Canadian goods hit by the US. The Canadian levies are set to come into effect on 8 September.It is the latest escalation after US-Canada trade talks collapsed late last week, with each side accusing the other of making last-minute demands that were unreasonable.Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said that Canada's retaliation is in response to 50% tariffs imposed by the Trump administration on a range of Canadian goods after trade talks fell apart on Friday."Those tariffs will have real consequences for Canadian workers, businesses and communities across our nation," he said. "Canada must respond."Champagne characterised Canada's retaliation as "proportionate" and "strategic".He added that Canada will also offer businesses and workers impacted by US tariffs an additional C$7.5bn for support programmes designed to minimise job losses and keep companies afloat.Placing taxes on trade between what are historically two of the world's closest trading partners will undoubtedly lead to pain on both sides of the border.Supply chains which have been developed over decades are set to see increased trading costs due the latest tariff announcements made from both the US and Canada, ultimately hitting businesses of all sizes and consumers through potentially higher prices.Polls suggest the majority of Canadians support their government in holding firm against the US. But some questions remain on exactly why trade talks fell apart, with the Conservative opposition asking that the full text of the draft deal with the US be released. Businesses have also expressed concerns about the impact of a prolonged trade war with Canada's largest trading partner.The White House released a statement after Canada announced its counter-tariffs, saying that the US was prepared to offer Canada "the most preferential market access of any country on Earth" in recent trade talks."Instead of partnership, Canada chose unreasonable demands, walk-backs, and flat-out rejection," it said.In a series of Tuesday posts on Truth Social, Trump also accused Canada of "ripping off" the US for decades and of charging American farmers steep tariffs. "I deal with many countries, and Canada is easily the most difficult and unreasonable," Trump wrote. "They feel entitled, but they are not a State, and will be entitled no longer!"He suggested that he will change the name of Lake Ontario, one of the Great Lakes on the US-Canada border, to Lake America, writing: "We don't expect to doing much business with Ontario any longer."Trump threatened this week to hike US tariffs on Canadian automobiles to 50% as of 1 January. Prime Minister Mark Carney responded by accusing Trump of wanting to "destroy" Canadian industries including the automobile manufacturing and steel and aluminum sectors. Public rhetoric on both sides reached a fever pitch on Monday, but some officials struck a more diplomatic tone on Tuesday with hopes that talks could be resumed.After calling Trump a "loser" on Monday at a news conference, Ontario Premier Doug Ford acknowledged in an interview with CNN that "things got a little heated"."But I want to make a deal — a good deal for the American people, a good deal for Canadians," Ford said.The escalation also puts into question the future of a North American free trade pact between Canada, the US and Mexico called the USMCA. President Claudia Sheinbaum had despatched her economy secretary, Marcelo Ebrard, to Washington for emergency talks after trade negotiations collapsed with Canada.

schema.headline: Canada announces 'dollar-for-dollar' retaliatory tariffs on US as high as 50%

title: LASK v Celtic: Martin O'Neill takes responsibility
description: O'Neill takes responsibility with nowhere to hide for CelticImage source, SNSImage caption, Celtic led LASK by four goals on aggregate, before losing
body: O'Neill takes responsibility with nowhere to hide for CelticImage source, SNSImage caption, Celtic led LASK by four goals on aggregate, before losing the tie 5-4ByScott MullenBBC Sport ScotlandIn the open air of the Raiffeisen Arena, with bedlam all around, there was nowhere to hide for Celtic or Martin O'Neill.The Scottish champions had endured one of the darkest nights in their European history. After going out to Kairat Almaty on penalties last year at this stage of the Champions League play-offs, that is saying something.Four goals up on aggregate against LASK, O'Neill's Celtic somehow conspired to implode in a second half with little sign of a response on the way to a 5-4 aggregate loss following extra time.There was no hiding place, and the Celtic manager was frank when put in the spotlight at full-time."I'm responsible for this one," he said."Without a doubt. Naturally it took me a long time to get over the Uefa Cup final in 2003 but this was majorly disappointing. "In the context of things, one was a final which it would have been terrific to win, this was a qualifying game which we should have been able to get through."We know that we are a million miles from the finished article. That's absolutely true. I think we thought that anyway."O'Neill was not in charge for that defeat in Kazakhstan a year ago as it triggered the start of the end for Brendan Rodgers' second spell at Celtic Park.The current Parkhead boss helped steady Celtic's ship last term following Rodgers' exit and again following the Wilfried Nancy saga to guide them to another league title and a Scottish Cup.This season appeared to get off to a prosperous start until the roof began to cave in over in Austria.Away from the raw pain of stumbling in such a stark way, the aftermath could be telling for Celtic who now have to not only pick themselves up, but finish off a transfer window without the hefty windfall which would have blown in with the Champions League."The qualification for the Champions League is major, it's major in every aspect," said O'Neill. "Financially, for prestige, but we have to pick ourselves up. That's my responsibility again to do that."I think I said last week that if you could qualify for the Champions League there would be players wanting to come on that basis. "That's not going to be the case but we'll see. Tonight we came up well and truly short, particularly in the second half."What the players saidCeltic captain Callum McGregor tells Amazon Prime: "We got what we deserved. We were passive all night. We looked scared to go and win the game."I didn't think we were that good in the first leg either. We scored at good times and got away with it."We have to suck it up. We apologise to our supporters and the club because there's no way we should lose that game."It's as much on the players as everyone else. You can't look for excuses elsewhere."You'll now see what people are made of. When you play like that you can't have any excuses whatsoever."When you go 1-0 up in the game and it still doesn't settle you, you can't have any excuse and that's on us."You fall at a big hurdle and these questions [on whether the squad are ready] are going to be asked. You can't lose by that margin then look for excuses elsewhere."This is what it's like to play at Celtic. You have to bounce back, you have to show a reaction and that's what Celtic are all about."The pundits viewFormer Celtic captain Scott Brown on BBC Radio Scotland: "It was a fantastic start, you go 1-0 up, but that seems like forever ago. Now they've crashed out the Champions League and conceded five goals."LASK outran Celtic in a couple of areas, the two up front were strong, solid and willing runners."LASK deserve to go through with that performance. I feel for the lads because I've been in that situation as well."Former Celtic manager Neil Lennon on Amazon Prime: "It looked to me as if Celtic were exhausted. Fragile in duels. It only looked like there would be one winner."Huge credit to LASK. "They battered Celtic tonight, physically and on the football side. It could have been more."Former Celtic midfielder Stiliyan Petrov: "Everyone [is to blame]. "They are all in it together. A big club like Celtic should be able to hold that out."

schema.headline: LASK v Celtic: Martin O'Neill takes responsibility

title: NFL: At least one in four dead players had brain disease, says study
description: As many as 97.7% of NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 could have had brain disease related to repeated blows to the head, a new study says.Re
body: As many as 97.7% of NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 could have had brain disease related to repeated blows to the head, a new study says.Researchers looked at 878 former players who died during that period, with 235 having donated their brains to research.Of those, 215 were found to have chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a degenerative brain disease which can only be diagnosed after death.The study, published in the British Medical Journal, external, also found dementia was common among brain donors."We and others have shown that in NFL players, specifically, there is about a four times higher rate of death from neurodegenerative disease than the general population," said the report's lead author Daniel Daneshvar, an associate professor at Harvard Medical School."These findings indicate that NFL players have a higher prevalence of CTE at death than has been previously shown in multiple community based studies." Researchers calculated a "conservative minimum" of CTE prevalence among those who died in the six-year period to be 24.5% - rising to a "maximum" 97.7%.They have urged the NFL to take prevention measures to reduce repetitive head impacts across all levels of the sport.

schema.headline: NFL: At least one in four dead players had brain disease, says study

title: Man dies in crash after Stratford-upon-Avon police pursuit
description: A man has died and two women have been injured in a crash after a police pursuit near Stratford-upon-Avon.Officers tried to stop a black Audi on Birmi
body: A man has died and two women have been injured in a crash after a police pursuit near Stratford-upon-Avon.Officers tried to stop a black Audi on Birmingham Road shortly before 17:30 BST on Monday but the driver failed to pull over, Warwickshire Police said.A pursuit began and 15 minutes later the Audi crashed into a white Ford Puma, the force added, with the Audi's 19-year-old male driver confirmed dead at the scene by paramedics. The driver of the Ford, a woman, was seriously injured and remains in hospital in critical condition, while injuries to a second woman - her passenger - were serious but not believed to be life-threatening. An investigation by the police watchdog is under way.Officers said after failing to stop, the Audi made off in the direction of the A46 before travelling back towards Stratford on the A439 Warwick Road where the crash occurred.A number of other cars were damaged during the pursuit, police said. Warwick Road was closed on Monday from the Marraway roundabout to its junction with Ingon Lane and Sand Barn Lane, with the stretch remaining shut on Tuesday morning.It later reopened. "We made a mandatory referral to the IOPC because a death had occurred following police contact. "They have declared an independent investigation and we will co-operate fully with their investigation."The IOPC said the investigation was at an early stage and confirmed its officials attended the police's post-incident operation to gather information. "We understand the driver of a black Audi A3 failed to stop for police and was then pursued for around six minutes before the vehicle was involved in a collision with a car being driven by a member of the public," a spokesperson said."We are also appealing for any car footage of the pursuit that other motorists may have recorded. Our investigators can be contacted at 0300 303 5609 or by email: WarwickRoadPursuit@policeconduct.gov.uk"We have met with the families of the driver and the seriously injured woman to explain our role and will keep them regularly updated throughout our investigation, which is at an early stage."Manuela Perteghella, Liberal Democrat MP for Stratford-on-Avon, said the incdent was "incredibly tragic". "My thoughts are with the families of all those impacted. We must now let the investigation take its course."Works were carried out on Warwick Road two years ago, aimed at reducing the number of crashes in the area.Warwickshire County Council added a one-way system, lowered the speed limit and implemented a protected turning lane at the Ingon Lane junction.Street lighting was also boosted to improve visibility for crossing pedestrians at Fisherman's Car Park.

schema.headline: Man dies in crash after Stratford-upon-Avon police pursuit

title: How Dolly Parton told her life story through six iconic songs
description: Figure caption, Watch: "We used flour for powder" - Dolly reflects on early life in 1979 BBC interviewByPaul GlynnCulture reporterCoat of Many ColorsI
body: Figure caption, Watch: "We used flour for powder" - Dolly reflects on early life in 1979 BBC interviewByPaul GlynnCulture reporterCoat of Many ColorsImage caption, Dolly Parton performed Coat of Many Colors on the BBC talk show Parkinson in 1979Let's start with Dolly Parton's own personal favourite, her 1971 acoustic country-folk ditty, Coat of Many Colors, external. The autobiographical track, taken from the album of the same name, tells the heart-stirring tale of how she grew up poor - as one of 12 siblings - but rich in love.In her book, Songteller: My Life in Lyrics, Parton described it as a "little story" that covers "a world of things", with teachings about bullying, acceptance, love and good parenting.The lyrics go: "Now I know we had no money, but I was rich as I could be / In my coat of many colors my momma made for me".The song has been covered by the likes of Shania Twain and Eva Cassidy, and Rolling Stone magazine put it in second place in its list of Parton's top 50 songs, external."Had it been the only song she'd ever written, the expression of overwhelming pride and crushing anguish... would have secured her indelible legacy," the US magazine wrote in 2023.Coat of Many Colors is also the title of Parton's own children's book, and a 2015 TV movie based on her life - starring Alyvia Alyn Lind as the precocious young singer dreaming of fame.Her mother, Avie Lee Parton, even made her daughter a new patchwork coat to put on display at the museum inside the Dollywood theme park in her home state of Tennessee.JoleneImage source, Michael Ochs Archives/Getty ImagesImage caption, Dolly Parton in 1974Parton penned many songs about all different aspects of her relationship with her devoted husband Carl Dean, who ran an asphalt paving business in Nashville.This included the fear that she might lose him, specifically to a red-headed bank clerk who had flirted with him early on in their marriage.We all know her by now, of course, as the infamous Jolene, external.With its fast fingerstyle minor riff, the song was nominated for a Grammy in 1974 and gave Parton her second number one single on the Billboard Hot Country Singles chart and her first foray into the main Hot 100 chart (60).It also showed Parton at her most vulnerable, making it all the more relatable. Instead of shedding tears or vowing revenge, we hear the protagonist in the song begging the mistress who holds the power to relinquish it."She got this terrible crush on my husband," Parton told US media in 2008. "And he just loved going to the bank because she paid him so much attention. It was kinda like a running joke between us - I was saying, 'Hell, you're spending a lot of time at the bank. I don't believe we've got that kind of money.'"Parton had met Dean outside a laundromat on the first day she arrived in Nashville as an 18-year-old aspiring singer. The pair were married for 60 years, until his death in 2025.A notoriously private man, he was "a little embarrassed" when she wrote Jolene, Parton said in a 2023 interview with BBC's The One Show, external, adding that "actually, it wasn't as serious [as it sounds]. I was just jealous 'cause she was a beautiful woman and he was just flirting."So it gave me a great idea for a song. There's always a Jolene in somebody's life."Figure caption, Dolly Parton: The life of a legendary country singerShe joked that later in life when she saw her, by now, much older husband snoozing in his chair at home, she thought Jolene "can have him now... where's Jolene when you need her?!"Jolene is her most popular song, having been streamed more than 913 million times on Spotify. Critics from Rolling Stone to the Guardian, external agree it's her best.Beyoncé gave it a modern rewrite for her 2024 Cowboy Carter, external album, changing the lyrics from: "I'm begging of you, please, don't take my man" to "I'm warning you, don't come for my man."I Will Always Love YouImage source, Michael Ochs Archives/Getty ImagesImage caption, The professional relationship between Dolly Parton and Porter Wagoner was a strong but complicated one, leading to her writing a goodbye song that doubles as a breakup balladDespite the romantic sounding title, this 1974 song, external is actually the sound of Parton tenderly asking her musical mentor, Porter Wagoner, to let her go and pursue her solo career.Parton was 21 when she joined Wagoner's variety TV show. They released a string of duets and toured together, leading fans to think they were an item.But they had a complicated relationship, with Parton later writing in another book, Star of the Show: My Life on Stage, that she felt Wagoner saw her rise as a "threat"."I was making my way as an artist, and he was already an established one. It was his show, but I was trying to grow in the business and grow as an artist myself."On the track we hear her sing: "Bittersweet memories / That is all I'm taking with me".Rough Trade's music blog, external once described it as being "heartwarming in its sentiment, crushing in its delivery."Elvis Presley was set to record a cover of the song in 1974, but Parton made the difficult decision to back out of the deal when his manager demanded half of the songwriting rights."I said, 'I can't do that'," she told Howard Stern in 2023. "Of course I cried all night about that."Parton re-recorded I Will Always Love You in 1982 for her starring role in the musical comedy film, The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas.But arguably the most iconic version comes courtesy of Whitney Houston who can be heard booming it out in another film, 1992's The Bodyguard. Her version remains the biggest-selling US single by a female artist.Parton said she heard the power ballad version for the first time on the radio, and felt so overwhelmed that she had to pull over to avoid crashing her Cadillac.Whitney Houston took her "little country song" and made it "so much more", she said.Light of a Clean Blue MorningWith Parton's newfound professional freedom came a renewed sense of hope, optimism and spirituality - as heard on her 1977 track, Light of a Clean Blue Morning.She recalled leaving Wagoner's office after their musical split and driving home in a rainstorm, until the clouds parted, giving way to sunlight and an idea for another new song.Parton - whose earliest performances were in church as a child - referred to it as her "song of deliverance", helping her on the road to stardom. The lyrics were reworked for the soundtrack to her 1992 romantic comedy film, Straight Talk.And in early 2026 she released a new charity version of the song, external, in aid of pediatric cancer research, featuring her goddaughter Miley Cyrus, Lainey Wilson, Queen Latifah and Reba.9 To 5Image source, Tom Wargacki/WireImageImage caption, Dolly Parton joined Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin at the 9 to 5 film premiere in 1980This defiant anthem of female empowerment, released in 1980, was the most transformative of her career.Already well established as a singer, 9 To 5, external brought Parton over into the mainstream popular culture.She wrote the country-tinged southern soul number as the theme tune for the comedy film of the same name, which saw her make her movie debut alongside Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin.It tells the story of three working women who live out their fantasies of getting even with, and overthrowing, their company's bigot of a boss (played by Dabney Coleman).The song's distinctive tapping beat at the start is none other than her acrylic nails: "I always play the nails and I'd come up with little things that I would see on the set, like 'I tumble out of bed and I stumble to the kitchen'… And I thought, 'Wow, that sounds like a typewriter,'" she once explained.Parton won two Grammys for the chart-topping tune, which was also nominated for an Oscar, and later spawned a Broadway musical and a documentary.Islands in the StreamImage source, Beth Gwinn/Redferns/ GettyImage caption, Parton said her collaboration with Kenny Rogers was one of the proudest things she had ever doneA modern day karaoke classic, Parton recorded this hit with fellow US country star Kenny Rogers, external as the lead single for his 1983 album, Eyes That See in the Dark.The deep love song sold millions of copies and topped both the country and pop charts at the same time.It was actually written for them by the Bee Gees, intended as a Motown-inspired duet. The Gibb brothers later recorded their own version and performed it live.Parton and Rogers' rendition, though, remains one of most popular country-pop duets of all time and a classic of the genre.Their collaboration was "another thing I'm as proud of as anything I ever did in my musical career," she told Smooth Radio, external 40 years on, in 2023.She added: "You want to do well and keeping up with the likes of Barry [Gibb] and Kenny [Rogers], but I just figure I'll just always be me and do me and that seems to work."Other notable song mentions:Down from Dover, external - the heartbreaking 1970 tale of an abandoned mother giving birth to a stillborn child was controversial and Wagoner warned Parton against releasing itThe Bargain Store, external - a moving lyrical account of a lady, experienced in love and loss, comparing herself to a secondhand shop, from 1975Here You Come Again, external - written by Barry Mann and Cynthia Weil and released by Parton in 1977, it saw her skillfully pivot to pop/soft rock to great effect on her first big crossover hit

schema.headline: How Dolly Parton told her life story through six iconic songs

title: Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 – the best pictures so far
description: A nosy polar bear and a lucky squirrel: Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 shortlistImage source, Audun RikardsenImage caption, This image titled
body: A nosy polar bear and a lucky squirrel: Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 shortlistImage source, Audun RikardsenImage caption, This image titled Icy Window was highly commended in the "Animal Portraits" categoryByMaddie MolloyClimate & Science reporterHow would it feel to find yourself face to face with one of the Arctic's most formidable predators?This stunning image captures life from a seal's perspective. Taken by Norwegian wildlife photographer Audun Rikardsen, it was among the 'Highly Commended' entries in this year's Wildlife Photographer of the Year competition.While working as a guide with Arctic Wildlife Tours, Rikardsen rigged an underwater camera with a motion sensor beneath a seal's breathing hole, and then waited. At 4am, a female polar bear approached and peered down.Rikardsen then waited eight hours for the bear to move away before retrieving the camera and reviewing the images. When he saw what he had captured, he said: "I was so extremely happy. I was screaming, so I probably woke up all the polar bears for miles."Rikardsen has previously won two Wildlife Photographer of the Year categories: Birds in 2019 and Oceans: The Bigger Picture in 2025. The overall winners will be announced on Tuesday 13 October 2026, followed by an exhibition at the Natural History Museum in London, external from Friday 16 October 2026.Scroll down to explore other highly commended works from the competition.Image source, Jack CrockfordTitle: The Art of Flying Photographer: Jack Crockford (UK)Category: Highly Commended, 15-17 Years Location: Bushy Park, LondonCrockford watched swifts return to London after their annual migration from Africa, filling the air with their high-pitched calls. Most flew too high to photograph, but a few lower-flying ones gave Crockford the opportunity to capture the picture he wanted. Swifts spend almost their entire lives in the air, usually landing only to nest.Image source, Sora MiyazawaTitle: Urban Wanderer  Photographer: Sora Miyazawa (Japan)Category: Highly Commended, 11-14 Years Location: Tokyo, JapanAfter rainfall, Miyazawa came across an Eastern Japanese toad making its way along a city street. He used a slow shutter speed to photograph it before it hopped back into the bushes. Eastern Japanese toads are typically found in forests, grasslands and other terrestrial habitats across eastern Japan, but they have also proved remarkably adaptable to urban environments.Image source, Vegard Byrkjeland AasenTitle: Lifted to the Surface Photographer: Vegard Byrkjeland Aasen (Norway)Category: Highly Commended, Behaviour: MammalsLocation: Kvænangen, Troms County, NorwayAasen was flying a drone for the Norwegian Orca Survey when he noticed an adult orca carrying the body of a deceased calf through a Norwegian fjord. The orca repeatedly allowed the calf to sink before bringing it back to the surface, a difficult moment to watch but one that Aasen felt was important to record. The behaviour may have been an attempt to revive or protect the calf. Killer whales have previously been observed carrying deceased calves, including a case where a female Southern Resident killer whale carried her dead calf for at least 17 days. A 2026 study, external suggests that this type of behaviour may be more widespread across the species than previously thought.Image source, Andrea & Maceo GrammaticoTitle: Biting Back Photographer: Andrea & Maceo Grammatico (France)Category: Highly Commended, Animal PortraitsLocation: Sierpe, South Puntarenas, Costa RicaOnly when they reviewed the images did the Grammatico twins realise they had captured a mosquito resting on the head of a fer-de-lance viper. They described it as "one of the most demanding focus stacks we've ever created". Highly venomous and responsible for more fatal snake bites in Central America than any other species, the fer-de-lance is well camouflaged and can blend into plantation habitats, sometimes going unnoticed by workers.Image source, Andrew ParkinsonTitle: Wings of Darkness Photographer: Andy Parkinson (UK)Category: Highly Commended, Animal PortraitsLocation: Meeting of the Waters State Park, Northern Pantanal, BrazilParkinson photographed a black vulture perched over a dead yacaré caiman in Brazil's Pantanal wetlands, keeping his boat at a distance and using a long telephoto lens to capture the shot.A jaguar waiting out of frame emerged after the vulture flew away to claim the carcass. Only then did Parkinson notice a suspiciously clean, straight wound on the back of the caiman's head, possibly caused by a blow from a speeding boat, he suspects.Image source, Dewald TrompTitle: Eye of the Storm Photographer: Dewald Tromp (South Africa)Category: Highly Commended, Animals in their EnvironmentLocation: Namib Desert, near Swakopmund, NamibiaTromp was photographing a Namaqua chameleon in the Namib Desert when the wind suddenly intensified, bringing a sandstorm that quickly reduced visibility and made breathing difficult. These chameleons are desert specialists and can obtain moisture directly from the air. Dew gathers on their skin and is channelled towards their mouths through microscopic grooves, while their tongues can also collect fog water condensed on plants, sand and rocks.Image source, Bence MátéTitle: Flock of Gold Photographer: Bence Máté (Hungary) - 2010 Wildlife Photographer winnerCategory: Highly Commended, Behaviour: BirdsLocation: Ashnil Aruba Lodge, Tsavo East National Park, KenyaMáté was watching birds gather at a small pond when tens of thousands of red-billed queleas swept down to drink in the golden late-afternoon light. The movement of so many wings created a rush of air that, he says, could be felt from 30m (98ft) away. Red-billed queleas can gather in flocks of up to two million and are considered the most abundant wild bird on Earth, with an estimated 1.5 billion breeding adults.Image source, Ernest PorterTitle: Mutual Friends Photographer: Ernest Porter (South Africa)Category: Highly Commended, Behaviour: BirdsLocation: Manyeleti Game Reserve, Mpumalanga, South AfricaWhile searching the reserve for wildlife, Porter photographed a red-billed oxpecker rubbing its bill against a white rhino's skin in the afternoon light. The birds feed on insects living on rhinos and can also act as sentinels - calling to warn their hosts when danger approaches. In Swahili, the red-billed oxpecker is known as askari wa kifaru, meaning "the rhino's guard".Image source, Allegra HuttonTitle: Up a Tree without a Squirrel Photographer: Allegra Hutton (USA)Category: Highly Commended, Behaviour: MammalsLocation: Okavango Delta, BotswanaHutton had watched a young leopard pursue a squirrel into a tree, having earlier seen the cat unsuccessfully attempt to stalk a rabbit. The squirrel escaped by climbing higher, leaving the leopard clinging on before it eventually made an awkward retreat. For young leopards, survival is far from guaranteed: fewer than half reach independence, with male leopards, lions and other predators among the threats they face.Image source, Jens CullmannTitle: Split-Second Escape  Photographer: Jens Cullmann (Germany)Category: Highly Commended, Behaviour: Amphibians and ReptilesLocation: Central Kalahari Game Reserve, BotswanaAn African bullfrog lunges for a babul butterfly but misses. Cullmann had noticed tadpoles on a previous visit after heavy rains and returned the following month to find ponds and puddles full of young bullfrogs. He spent more than two weeks watching the young frogs "eat everything that moved". As adults, African bullfrogs can reach 12cm (4.7in) in length and spend around 10 months of the year dormant underground, emerging after the rains to breed and feed voraciously.Image source, Gil WizenTitle: Hidden Dragon  Photographer: Gil Wizen (Israel/Canada)Category: Highly Commended, Behaviour: InvertebratesLocation: Wildsumaco Biological Station, Napo Province, EcuadorWizen was photographing a lichen dragon katydid measuring just 15mm long, making it difficult to distinguish from the lichen around it. He spotted the insect when it moved, but even then struggled to separate it from its background through the viewfinder. Found only in Ecuador's Andes Mountains, its spiny armour helps protect it from eagle-eyed predators that can see through its disguise.Image source, Shane GrossTitle: Calm Amid the Storm Photographer: Shane Gross (Canada) - 2024 Wildlife Photographer winnerCategory: Highly Commended, Oceans: The Bigger Picture Location: D'Arros Island, SeychellesGross was photographing a school of bigeye trevally near the shore at sunrise as a storm approached. To create a split-level image, he turned his camera upside down to aid buoyancy distribution and slowly moved towards the curious fish.Bigeye trevally are fished in many parts of the world, but here they are relatively safe. In 2023, the waters surrounding D'Arros Island were made a Marine Protected Area and designated as a no-take zone as part of the worldwide initiative for governments to protect 30% of Earth's land and ocean by 2030.Image source, Loren ElliottTitle: Pooltime Pastime Photographer: Loren Elliott (USA)Category: Highly Commended, Urban WildlifeLocation: Monrovia, California, USAElliott spent hours watching through the kitchen window of a local resident's home, hoping to photograph black bears that frequently pass through the garden. He observed one stopping for a dip in the garden pool, highlighting the increasingly common overlap between wildlife and residential life in Los Angeles County, where housing developments have spread into bear habitat.Image source, Ralph PaceTitle: Ocean Protector Photographer: Ralph Pace (USA) - 2025 Underwater category winner Category: Highly Commended, Wetlands: The Bigger PictureLocation: Monterey Bay, California, USAA sea hare glides through an eelgrass meadow in the shallows of Monterey Bay, where Pace was photographing in the evening light. He saw the encounter as a hopeful image of "a gentle giant safeguarding the last green meadows of the sea". By grazing on red algae, that can prevent sunlight reaching the meadow, sea hares play a role in restoring eelgrass, which is vital to coastal ecosystems and an important carbon sink.Image source, Pietro RojasTitle: The Show Goes On Photographer: Pietro Rojas (Guatemala)Category: Highly Commended, PhotojournalismLocation: Doha, QatarAfter learning that a circus featuring animal acts was in town, Rojas went to document it and saw a brown bear riding a small motorcycle, muzzled and secured to the apparatus. For him the scene highlighted the contrast between the animal's wild nature and the human environment imposed upon it. More than 50 countries around the world have now banned or restricted the use of wild animals in circuses, over concerns it causes them distress, external.Wildlife Photographer of the Year is developed and produced by the Natural History Museum, London.

schema.headline: Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 – the best pictures so far

title: CIA chief travels to Moscow for unannounced talks, US media reports
description: The head of the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) has travelled to Moscow for unannounced talks, the BBC's US news partner CBS has reported.John Ra
body: The head of the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) has travelled to Moscow for unannounced talks, the BBC's US news partner CBS has reported.John Ratcliffe reportedly arrived in the Russian capital earlier on Tuesday. Neither Washington or Moscow have confirmed the nature of the visit or who he was due to meet.In-person talks between high-level American and Russian officials are rare.Flight tracking data confirmed a large US military aircraft travelled to Russia from the US via Latvia on Tuesday. It departed later on Tuesday.BBC News has contacted the CIA, the White House and Pentagon for comment. Footage posted on social media showed the C-17 transport plane approaching Moscow's Vnukovo international airport.It departed Riga airport at 05:50 GMT and appeared to have landed in the Russian capital at around 07:04 GMT, according to data from FlightRadar24. It returned to Riga shortly before 17:00 GMT.Footage on social media also purported to show a diplomatic motorcade travelling through Moscow.Ahead of the trip, the US told Ukraine that a senior delegation would be travelling to Moscow and asked Kyiv to suspend strikes until they had left, a senior Ukrainian official told CBS.The trip is thought to be Ratcliffe's first trip to Russia as CIA director, although he has maintained contact with his intelligence counterparts in Moscow.John Foreman, who served as a British military attaché to Moscow between 2019 and 2022, told Radio 4's PM programme that the visit could be focused on "escalation management" given speculation recent drone activity in Germany could be linked to Russia.He said: "The Americans don't normally send such a high ranking official to Moscow unannounced at short notice unless something is up."Foreman said the trip could also concern the release of US detainees currently being held in Russia.Ratcliffe played a role in negotiations for the release of Russian-American citizen Ksenia Karelina, who was jailed in Russia for over a year after being accused of providing support to Ukraine. The CIA was also involved in a 2024 prisoner swap deal with Russia that saw the release of Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich, as well as former US marine Paul Whelan and Russian-American journalist Alsu Kurmasheva.The US has had strained relations with Russia since it launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Since then, Russia has been isolated on the world stage and faced international economic sanctions.Ratcliffe appears to be one of the highest-ranking US officials to visit the country during President Donald Trump's second term.Trump met Russian President Vladimir Putin at a summit in Alaska last year but the meeting did not lead to a breakthrough. Subsequent US-led peace talks between Russia and Ukraine appear to have stalled.Additional reporting by Washington correspondent Daniel Bush and BBC Verify

schema.headline: CIA chief travels to Moscow for unannounced talks, US media reports

title: Nicotine vapes best chance to quit smoking, major review finds
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByMichelle RobertsDigital health editorSmokers who want to quit have the best chance of doing so if they use nicotine e-ciga
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByMichelle RobertsDigital health editorSmokers who want to quit have the best chance of doing so if they use nicotine e-cigarettes, a review has found. The Cochrane team looked at 80 major trials involving nearly 30,000 people and found that nicotine vapes were more effective than traditional aids such as patches, gum and support plans - increasing the success rate by about 60%, from around six in every 100 managing to quit smoking to one in every 10.They outperformed non-nicotine vapes too, although researchers say switching to these afterwards might help with weaning off nicotine.And they could prove more effective than the new anti-smoking pill cytisine, external, which the NHS has started to roll out - although more research is needed.Long-term risks not yet clear Experts say vaping, although not entirely risk-free, is far safer than smoking. In the UK, there are now more over-16s using vapes or e-cigarettes than smoking cigarettes, figures show. Around 5.3 million people or 10% of adults say they smoke, while around 5.4 million use vapes daily or occasionally.The review, external of the most recent and best quality evidence to date applies to regulated vapes that are checked for quality and compliant with strict safety laws. It doesn't look at unregulated ones that can contain illicit substances, like spice or THC. One of the report authors, Dr Jamie Hartmann-Boyce, cautioned: "Unlicensed e-cigarettes are potentially dangerous, with issues including unstable batteries and harmful chemicals. "Anyone looking to use e-cigarettes to quit smoking should only purchase devices that have been tested and approved by their country's regulatory body."The review found no evidence of any increased risk of serious harm from using e-cigarettes to quit.The long-term risks of vaping are not yet clear though, and the NHS says children and non-smokers should never vape. Doctors say vaping could lead to health harms in children and should be made "less attractive" to them. Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Smoking is the leading cause of preventable disease and death, killing over seven million a yearAround two in three people who smoke long-term will die from a tobacco-related illness, says the charity Action on Smoking and Health. According to the World Health Organization, smoking is the leading cause of preventable disease and death, killing over seven million people a year. Quitting smoking reduces your risk of serious illnesses like heart disease, lung cancer, and stroke. Almost every local NHS stop smoking service provides vapes or other support to help people quit.You can search online, external for your local service with your postcode.

title: Dolly Parton obituary: The country legend who sang from the heart
description: Dolly Parton: Life of the music legend whose songs touched millionsFigure caption, Dolly Parton: The life of a legendary country singerByTiffany Werth
body: Dolly Parton: Life of the music legend whose songs touched millionsFigure caption, Dolly Parton: The life of a legendary country singerByTiffany Wertheimer and Emma PetrieDolly Parton, the country singer from the Smoky Mountains of Tennessee, will be remembered for her songs that told beautiful stories so honestly, such as Coat of Many Colors, Jolene and I Will Always Love You.In a seven-decade career, Parton won 10 Grammy awards, sold more than 100 million records worldwide, and wrote in excess of 3,000 songs.Parton took her writing seriously, and considered herself a songwriter over everything else. "It's my way of expressing myself," she said. "It's my therapy.”She was also a savvy businesswoman who wasn't afraid to make tough decisions. Armed with a quick wit and southern charm, she took control of her showbusiness career that spanned more than 60 years.Image source, Getty Images/Michael Ochs ArchivesImage caption, Dolly Parton aged nineDolly Rebecca Parton was born in 1946, the fourth of 12 children, into a poor farming family who lived in a one-bedroom cabin in Tennessee.   Her father, Robert Lee Parton, was a tobacco farmer and paid a missionary a sack of cornmeal for delivering her.There was already music in the family - her mother, Avie Lee, sang folk songs all the time and her aunt played the guitar and wrote songs. During some of Parton's earliest performances, her uncle, Bill Owens, accompanied her on the guitar - formative years for the future music legend.From the age of six, she sang in the local church where her grandfather was the pastor, and was performing on her local TV station by the time she was a teenager.In 1959, when she was 13 years old, Parton performed with Uncle Bill at the Grand Ole Opry in Nashville - a live broadcast that is regarded as country music's biggest stage.She was introduced by Johnny Cash and received three encores.Image source, Getty Images//Michael Ochs ArchivesImage caption, Nineteen-year-old Dolly Parton in Nashville, 1965The 'town tramp'During her teenage years, Parton began to model herself on a local character who was known as the “town tramp”.  The lady wore bright red nail polish, low-cut tops and high heels - young Dolly thought she was beautiful.  When people said to her: “She ain’t nothing but trash”, Parton would reply: "Well, that’s what I’m gonna be when I grow up”.Parton sang “I’m just a backwards Barbie / too much make-up, too much hair”, but her image was both a coat of armour and an astute disguise that helped get her noticed in showbusiness. She would get ahead of the jokes by making them first, and had a quick and simple response for anyone who suggested she should tone it down: "Go to hell."Image source, Getty Images/CBS photo ArchiveImage caption, Parton said she felt better in bright colours and shiny clothes on stage: "You'd be surprised how much it costs to look this cheap"After graduating from high school in 1964, she moved to Nashville to launch her singing career and met her future husband, Carl Dean, on her very first day.They married two years later and remained together until his death in 2025.In Nashville, Parton's singing caught the eye of country performer Porter Wagoner, who hired her to perform on his television programme.Over the next seven years, the pair became one of country music's most popular duos, releasing so many duets that many fans assumed they were a couple.But their relationship was a complicated one, and as Parton's solo career started to rise, so did tensions behind the scenes.Writing in her book Star of the Show: My Life on Stage, Parton said Wagoner saw her success away from his show as a "threat".Image source, Getty Images/Michael Ochs ArchivesImage caption, Dolly Parton with Porter Wagoner on the set of his TV show in 1967While travelling with Wagoner on a tour bus in 1969, Parton wrote Coat of Many Colors, a beautifully emotive tale of how she grew up poor, but rich with love. Scrawled on the back of one of Wagoner's dry cleaning receipts, it was rated by Rolling Stone magazine, external as her second best-ever song. Years later, Parton named her own children's book Coat of Many Colors, and it was the name of a 2015 TV movie based on her life."It's a song that's just stood by me... it's created a life of many colours for me," she said.Image source, Getty Images/Ethan MillerImage caption, Dolly Parton won several awards for her made-for-TV movie Coat of Many Colors'Sad little country song'Despite being unable to read sheet music, Parton played several instruments including the banjo, harp, piano and saxophone.She had her first number one hit - and first Grammy nomination - with the song Joshua in 1971 and finally left The Porter Wagoner Show in 1974 to concentrate on her solo career.To say goodbye to him, she wrote I Will Always Love You, a song that many think is about two lovers parting ways."That's the prettiest song I ever heard," Wagoner cried when he first heard it, her website says.The same year, Elvis Presley was set to record a cover of the song, but Parton pulled the deal when his manager demanded half of the songwriting rights.She cried all night at the difficult decision, and Priscilla Presley later told her that Elvis sang the song to her during their divorce.In 1992, Whitney Houston transformed it into a now-iconic power ballad. Parton said she was driving when she first heard the cover and had to pull over: “When I heard her go from the a cappella into the music part, I honestly thought I was going to have a heart attack, it was one of the most overwhelming things.”Houston's cover of Parton's “sad little country song” was one of the proudest moments of her life, she said.Parton re-recorded the song for The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas, a 1982 film in which she starred and was nominated for a Golden Globe for best actress.That other womanAnother of her most famous songs was released in 1974 - Jolene.Showing her aching vulnerability, it's about a bank clerk with flaming locks of auburn hair who flirted with her husband."Jolene, I'm begging of you, please don't take my man," she pleads.Parton said her husband, who was notoriously private, was a bit embarrassed by the song. But it was nothing serious - just a running joke between them: "I was saying, 'Hell, you're spending a lot of time at the bank. I don't believe we've got that kind of money.'"The song has been covered by many artists including The White Stripes, Miley Cyrus and Beyoncé, who changed up the lyrics to the more ominous: "I'm warning you, don't come for my man." In the years to come, Dolly Parton's success only grew, with more hits, nominations and awards - she won her first Grammy in 1978 for Here You Come Again. Image source, Richard McCaffrey/Michael Ochs ArchiveImage caption, "If you see someone without a smile, give 'em one of yours": Parton performing in California in 1978Playing her acrylic nailsIt was the theme song that Dolly Parton wrote for the 1980 movie 9 to 5 that fully propelled her to stardom.Actress Jane Fonda, who produced and starred in the film about women being discriminated against in the workplace, made a deal with Parton - she'd star in the film if she could also write the theme song.Realising her nails clicking together sounded like a typewriter, she wrote 9 to 5 while waiting around on set. Fonda said she realised straight away that it wasn't just a theme song - it was an anthem.The film was a big success at the box office and the song won several awards, including a Golden Globe.Image source, Getty Images/Michael Ochs ArchivesImage caption, Jane Fonda, Lily Tomlin and Dolly Parton in a scene from 9 to 5'I look like a woman but I think like a man'Parton was a successful and shrewd businesswoman, and in 2022 was listed by Forbes as one of America's richest self-made women, external."I look like a woman but I think like a man. I've done business with men who think I'm as silly as I look. By the time they realise I'm not, I've got the money and gone," she once said.Her physical appearance - the costumes, wigs, long painted nails and high heels - were merely a facade of a stereotypical “dumb blonde”. But she always said she knew she wasn't dumb "and I also know that I'm not blonde".She had her own record label, Dolly Records, and co-owned The Dollywood Company, which manages entertainment venues, a theme park, a water park and a resort.In 1986, she opened her Dollywood amusement park in the foothills of her beloved Smoky Mountains. As well as rollercoasters, it is home to the largest sanctuary for non-releasable bald eagles in the world. Its rehabilitation and breeding work has won awards and in 2007, the bald eagle was removed from the endangered species list.Image source, Ron Galella, Ltd./Ron Galella Collection via Getty ImagesImage caption, Parton, pictured at Dollywood in 1993, said she wanted to build a place where the culture of the Smoky Mountains could be celebratedDespite her wealth and success, Parton remained humble and supported the communities where she grew up.Inspired by her father who couldn’t read or write, she launched the Imagination Library in 1999, which gave free books to children in Tennessee. It has since expanded to Australia, the UK, Ireland and Canada, sending out millions of free books every year.Her non-profit organisation, The Dollywood Foundation, has funded scholarships, hospitals and donated to flood and wildfire victims.In 2020, as the Covid-19 pandemic gripped the world, Parton donated $1m (£716,000) to the Vanderbilt University Medical Centre which helped to fund the Moderna vaccine. In later years, Parton had to postpone or cancel several shows for health treatment.In May 2026, she postponed an upcoming Las Vegas residency because of treatment for kidney stones, saying it would take some time to heal and be "stage-performance ready"."I can't be dizzy carrying around banjos, guitars and such on five-inch heels - and you know that I'm going to be wearing them," she said in a video message. "Not to mention all those heavy rhinestone outfits, the big hair, my big... uh, personality," she joked.Image source, Brandon Sloter/Image Of Sport/Getty ImagesImage caption, Parton amazed fans when she performed at the NFL Thanksgiving half-time show in 2023, aged 77Parton spoke graciously throughout her career with humour and intelligence. She steered clear of politics, saying she didn't want to alienate half her audience. She was a courageous and talented trailblazer for country music at a time when women were not taken seriously in the industry, especially as solo artists.Parton said she hoped to be remembered for her songwriting and as somebody who took her work seriously, but not herself.She once offered this advice: “Never ignore your roots, your home, or your hair."It's guidance that she stayed true to throughout her life.

schema.headline: Dolly Parton obituary: The country legend who sang from the heart

title: Trump hopes sanctions will topple Iran's regime - its leaders are betting otherwise
description: The US says it has launched an "economic onslaught against Iran's financial connections around the globe". Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said sanct
body: The US says it has launched an "economic onslaught against Iran's financial connections around the globe". Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said sanctions included digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping. Any nation financially partnering with Iran would be isolated.However, Bessent's announcement of what he termed an "economic D-Day" may have sounded more dramatic in Washington than in Tehran.Shortly after the announcement, Iran's Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh called it "the same old talk" and said Iran was ready for "every scenario". He said Tehran had expected the measures and had plans to deal with them.His reaction points to the main question Iranian leaders are likely to be asking: What can the US do now that it has not already tried?Bessent has threatened wider secondary sanctions against countries, banks and companies that continue doing business with Iran. But the basic policy is not new. Iran has faced US sanctions for years, including penalties against foreign companies trading with it.What matters to Tehran is whether Washington can enforce sanctions more widely than before.The US blockade has already made a difference. It has reduced Iran's ability to export as much oil by sea as it did before and made it harder to import goods and equipment. Iran has long land borders with seven countries and years of experience using them to bypass sanctions. But land routes cannot easily replace trade by sea, especially oil exports.The pressure could therefore become much more serious if Washington manages to close channels that survived previous sanctions, particularly those involving China and Iran's neighbours. That is a big ask. China's foreign ministry said on Tuesday that it firmly opposed the sanctions, calling them illegal.If the sanctions fail, Bessent's announcement could strengthen those inside Iran who oppose a deal with the US.They could argue that Washington has returned to economic pressure because its other choices are limited. A new military campaign carries risks, while years of sanctions have failed to force Iran to accept US demands.Washington has also left little room for diplomacy. Although Pakistan and other mediators are still trying to revive talks, the US has not ruled out further strikes. The renewed threats could weaken Iranian officials who favour a deal.It was already in deep trouble before the war, with high inflation and a rapidly weakening currency, and has deteriorated further since the fighting began with US and Israeli air strikes on 28 February. The weakening of the Iranian currency, the  rial, is felt sharply and widely. Imports cost more, businesses struggle to plan, and people's savings lose value. Restrictions on oil exports also reduce the government's access to foreign currency. Negin - not her real name - is a 34-year-old woman who says her monthly income is now about  $100 (£73). She told the BBC: "I don't go to the cinema, theatre, or concerts. I don't buy gifts for anyone. I don't attend birthday parties. I can only buy meat with the government subsidy voucher; otherwise, I wouldn't be able to afford it."Mona, a housewife with two kids, says her husband has been out of work since the beginning of the war. She adds: "We feel scared, especially after the sanctions that began yesterday. Ever since the war, my spouse has not gone back to work. He used to work on ships."She adds: "We're trying to manage our expenses as best we can, but we've definitely had to cut back on all of our extra spending and small luxuries."Iran may believe time is working against US President Donald Trump. Further disruption in the Strait of Hormuz could push oil and petrol prices higher, add to US inflation and become a political problem before the US midterm elections in November. That gives Tehran an obvious date to watch, but relying on American elections is a gamble.Iran's economy could be much weaker by then. And beyond the midterms lies another problem. With Trump not seeking re-election in 2028, his outgoing administration may feel it has more freedom to continue the confrontation with Iran and accept the costs.Iran is, therefore, watching two clocks.One is political and runs in Washington. The other is economic and runs inside Iran. Every month of lower oil exports, disrupted trade and pressure on the rial makes waiting for a deal to end the war more expensive.That leaves Iranian leaders with a difficult choice. Making concessions now could look like surrendering under pressure and strengthen hardliners who say Washington will only demand more.Waiting could improve Iran's position if Trump's strategy runs into political or economic problems. But Tehran could also find itself negotiating later with a weaker economy.Much now depends on what happens outside Iran.If Chinese banks, regional trading partners and companies start pulling back because they believe Washington will punish them, Bessent's campaign may change Tehran's calculation.If they do not, the opposite could happen. Those Iranians arguing against compromise will say Washington has played another supposedly decisive card without changing the balance and that Iran should continue to wait or resist.

schema.headline: Trump hopes sanctions will topple Iran's regime - its leaders are betting otherwise

title: Spanish government says sorry to people of Ceuta for migrant crisis
description: The Spanish government has apologised to the people of Ceuta for the migrant crisis that has affected the city for weeks and it has unveiled plans to
body: The Spanish government has apologised to the people of Ceuta for the migrant crisis that has affected the city for weeks and it has unveiled plans to overhaul the country's immigration laws."I want to apologise to all those who may have felt, or who even still feel, abandoned or not sufficiently cared for," Defence Minister Margarita Robles told a parliamentary committee."I have witnessed first-hand your feelings of anxiety, of abandonment, of lack of safety."At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta, a Spanish exclave in North Africa on 30 and 31 July. Most of the migrants swam around the border fence and at least 100 people died during the mass crossing, according to figures from Ceuta's mayor, Juan Jesús Vivas.The vast majority of the migrants returned to Morocco within hours of their arrival, but several thousand remain in Ceuta, many of them children, and most sleeping rough on beaches or streets.The Socialist government of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has been under mounting pressure to resolve the situation, with many residents and the local authorities in Ceuta, which has a population of 84,000, complaining that it is unsustainable.The Sánchez government has now declared a situation of interest for national security in the city, centralising management of the crisis. Territorial Policy Minister Ángel Víctor Torres has been tasked with co-ordinating the response, relieving the Ceuta local government of that responsibility.Coinciding with the government's moves and Robles's parliamentary appearance – the first by ministers on this issue over the coming days – changes were also announced to migration and asylum legislation.Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said the reforms would seek to ensure Spain that was fully in line with new EU regulations and that its process was "orderly, efficient, and... [provided] all possible guarantees". It will include limiting to three days the amount of time an undocumented migrant can spend undergoing medical, biometric and legal evaluation on arrival – EU regulations allow this period to last up to seven days.The reforms will also create a two-speed system for processing asylum requests, in theory accelerating cases deemed urgent.However, the information provided by government ministers has left some questions unanswered. Robles told parliament that agents of the CNI intelligence service had shared information about a possible imminent migrant crossing with security forces shortly before it happened, but Grande-Marlaska appeared to contradict her."There was no report that hinted that on 30 July what eventually happened was going to happen," he said. Robles later said that the information had not been conveyed via a report.Sánchez has blamed traffickers and social media activity for the mass crossing. However, many others have pointed the finger at Morocco, which in the past has been accused of using the borders with Ceuta and its sister city Melilla to pressure Madrid or the EU on political issues.

schema.headline: Spanish government says sorry to people of Ceuta for migrant crisis

title: As Ukraine hits Russia's refineries, Russia targets Ukraine's petrol pumps
description: "Fill up quickly and move on," Mayor Ihor Terekhov warns drivers in Ukraine's second largest city Kharkiv.Two petrol stations in the city in Ukraine's
body: "Fill up quickly and move on," Mayor Ihor Terekhov warns drivers in Ukraine's second largest city Kharkiv.Two petrol stations in the city in Ukraine's north-east were hit by Russian drones on Monday, which local officials say wounded two people. In another attack on a petrol station outside the city of Kryvyi Rih last week, three people were killed.Russia's campaign of targeting civilian filling stations with drones and missiles began in earnest in April, primarily in regions on the front line, and the attacks are steadily growing more frequent.At the same time, Russia has endured two waves of severe fuel shortages across the country as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries.In total, Russia has hit at least 246 filling stations across Ukraine so far, says Oleksandr Sirenko, an analyst with Ukrainian energy think-tank Nafto Rynok ("Oil Market").In July alone, the Centre for Information Resilience, an open-source investigation non-profit group, verified 114 Russian strikes on filling stations, compared with 66 the month before.Given the threat, police have issued special guidance urging motorists to leave petrol stations and, if necessary, to abandon their vehicles whenever air raid alerts sound. "You can fix your car, but you won't get your life back," says one police force in the Dnipropetrovsk region.The damage is highly disruptive and puts civilians at considerable risk.According to Sirenko, initially the attacks were being carried out with smaller, remote-controlled drones, but then Russia started using bigger, more expensive and more destructive Iranian-made Shahed drones.One Shahed drone is estimated to cost between $20,000 (£14,500) and $50,000 (£36,000)."One petrol station took five Shahed hits," Sirenko tells the BBC. "These Shaheds cost more than the petrol station."Some key roads have no functioning petrol stations left, such as the road linking the two major cities of Kharkiv and Dnipro.All the petrol stations have been destroyed around Opishnya, a large village in neighbouring Poltava region."You can see our enemy's strategy. They want to deprive us of fuel," says village chief Mykola Riznyk. In a video on Facebook, he says local authorities have begun stocking up on fuel, keeping small amounts of it in different locations.In Mykolaiv in southern Ukraine, local resident and driver Kateryna Stokolya says petrol stations everywhere are becoming far stricter about not working during air alerts."Now everyone's making allowances for that, and it's not a problem," she tells the BBC. "Security comes first. If you can't fill up now, you'll fill up later. There are no queues or panic buying."Stokolya believes that, in carrying out attacks of this nature, Russia's intended goal is "terrorising the public so we force the government to capitulate or accept agreements that do not favour Ukraine".In Ukrainian-controlled areas of the partly occupied Kherson region, almost half the petrol stations have stopped working. The others get attacked by Russian drones "almost every day", says deputy regional administration head Oleksandr Tolokonnikov.All petrol stations have reportedly been destroyed in Trostyanets, a town of almost 20,000 people near the north-eastern border with Russia. In response, local authorities started dispensing fuel straight from road tankers which keep changing their location to minimise the chances of being hit.Ukrainians appear to be heeding the advice of authorities."Clients aren't browsing the aisles anymore, looking at what we've got on our shelves," says Oleksandr Melnychuk, head of the strategic marketing department at BRSM Nafta chain of petrol stations. "They fill up and are keen to get on their way as soon as possible."His company has lost eight petrol stations and is rebuilding another two after they were hit.To protect customers, BRSM Nafta has been building concrete shelters at its forecourts and also covering them in anti-drone nets. It has also shortened working hours and reduced the number of staff present in some locations.However, so far the drone strikes have not had a dramatic impact on fuel supplies. According to a report by the National Bank of Ukraine, 4% of the country's filling stations have been damaged or destroyed, but the impact on the market has been small."Increasing sales in regions which are further away from the front line or from the border with Russia have made up for sales lost at destroyed stations," the report says.The picture in Russia is very different, after Ukraine's campaign of attacks on Russian refineries and other infrastructure.Russia has seen fuel shortages in almost every region as a result. One popular newspaper in Russia, Izvestia, said last week that petrol was only available at 28% of Russian filling stations.Unlike in Russia, Ukraine does not rely on vulnerable large refineries and fuel depots, instead importing fuel by road using tanker trucks.Ukraine's market is also saturated with numerous petrol stations, which usually offer drivers alternatives should one or several of them be targeted in a particular area, Sirenko says."You curse and drive on to another petrol station. OK, you travel for 10km more than you bargained for, but that's not such a big problem," he says.If anything, it is the war between the US and Iran that is having a bigger impact on local fuel prices, he says. Normally, the most expensive parts of filling stations are left undamaged by Russian attacks, such as petrol and diesel tanks underground.

schema.headline: As Ukraine hits Russia's refineries, Russia targets Ukraine's petrol pumps
